content: Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), has emphasized the importance of optimizing community health worker (CHW) programs to strengthen the connection between health systems and communities. However, several barriers hinder the achievement of these goals. These include a shortage of health workers, uneven distribution of health workers and facilities, limited access to health services for vulnerable populations, low quality of care, and inadequate training, supervision, and support for health workers. The WHO Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 encourages countries to adopt a diverse and sustainable mix of skills, leveraging the potential of community-based and mid-level health workers as part of inter-professional primary care teams. The WHO has developed evidence-based policy guidance to support national strategies and investments in building a community-based health workforce that is fit for purpose. Effective CHW programs are expected to increase coverage of essential health services, improve equity in access, and reduce deaths, illnesses, and disease burdens. Community health workers play a critical role in delivering preventive, promotional, and curative health services. They help reduce inequities in access to care, generate employment opportunities (especially for women), and contribute to economic growth and broader development outcomes. CHWs are involved in various health interventions, including the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of communicable diseases like malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, as well as non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and asthma. They also provide maternal and newborn health services, mental health support, and public health education. Despite their recognized potential, support for CHWs and their integration into health systems and communities remains inconsistent across and within countries. Successful CHW programs require evidence-based models for their education, deployment, and management. The WHO guideline aims to assist governments and partners in improving the design, implementation, performance, and evaluation of CHW programs, contributing to the progressive realization of universal health coverage. The guideline focuses on three key areas of policy interventions for CHWs: selection, education, and certification; management and supervision; and integration into and support by health systems and communities. Recommendations include selecting CHWs based on educational qualifications, community acceptance, personal attributes, and gender equity. Pre-service training should be tailored to the expected roles and responsibilities of CHWs, balancing theoretical knowledge with practical skills. Supportive supervision, appropriate remuneration, clear contracting agreements, and career progression opportunities are also essential for the success of CHW programs. Integrating CHWs into health systems and gaining community support are critical for optimizing their impact. This involves engaging communities in defining needs, selecting CHWs, and holding them accountable. CHWs should also be enabled to collect and use health data effectively while minimizing reporting burdens. The WHO guideline highlights the importance of embedding CHW programs within the broader health system, aligning them with national health policies and workforce strategies. Investments in CHW programs are essential to achieving Sustainable Development Goal 3, as they represent a cost-effective approach to addressing health system challenges. Countries at all levels of socioeconomic development have demonstrated the feasibility of prioritizing large-scale CHW initiatives. The guideline also acknowledges gaps in evidence, particularly regarding certification, contracting, career ladders, and economic evaluations of CHW interventions. Addressing these gaps through research and long-term studies will help refine CHW program policies and improve their effectiveness. The WHO launched this guideline in October 2018 during the Global Conference on Primary Health Care, marking the 40th anniversary of the Declaration of Alma-Ata, which recognized CHWs as a vital component of primary care. The evolving role of CHWs should be considered in the context of long-term changes in population health needs and health system requirements. Policymakers are encouraged to adopt a whole-of-system approach, ensuring that CHW programs are integrated into the overall health system and aligned with national priorities. The WHO invites countries, partners, and stakeholders to engage in policy dialogue, share experiences, and champion the implementation of these guidelines to optimize CHW programs and advance global health goals.
